rewritten_text:
Recent reports from Rotterdam suggest that the city is in a state of intense scientific excitement. Indeed, events have occurred there so completely unexpected—so entirely unfamiliar—so utterly opposed to accepted ideas—that I have no doubt all Europe is already in an uproar, all physics in turmoil, and reason and astronomy locked together in a quarrel.

It appears that on the —— day of —— (I cannot be certain of the date), an enormous crowd had gathered, for reasons not specifically stated, in the great Exchange square in the prosperous city of Rotterdam. The day was warm—unusually warm for the season—and scarcely a breath of air moved. The people were quite happy to be sprinkled from time to time by welcome, brief showers falling from the great white clouds that irregularly patterned the blue dome of the sky. Nevertheless, around noon, a slight but noticeable disturbance began to spread through the gathering. The chatter of ten thousand tongues followed; an instant later, ten thousand faces turned upward, ten thousand pipes dropped simultaneously from the corners of ten thousand mouths, and a shout comparable only to the roar of Niagara echoed long, loud, and furious throughout the surrounding districts of Rotterdam.

The cause of this commotion soon became clear enough. From behind the enormous bulk of one of those sharply outlined clouds, something was seen slowly emerging into a clear expanse of blue. It was a strange assortment of parts, apparently solid, so oddly shaped and fancifully assembled that the sturdy citizens standing openmouthed below could neither understand it in the least nor ever admire it enough. What could it be? In the name of all the wives and devils in Rotterdam, what on earth could it mean? Nobody knew; nobody could imagine. Nobody—not even the mayor, Mynheer Superbus Von Underduk—possessed the slightest clue that might unravel the mystery. So, since there was nothing more sensible to be done, every last man carefully returned his pipe to the corner of his mouth and, turning his right eye up toward the apparition, puffed, paused, waddled about, and grunted meaningfully—then waddled back, grunted, paused, and finally—puffed again.

Meanwhile, however, the object of so much curiosity, and the cause of so much smoke, descended lower and lower toward the handsome city. Within a very few minutes it had come close enough for its details to be clearly seen. It appeared to be—yes! There could be no doubt that it was a kind of balloon; but certainly nobody in Rotterdam had ever seen a balloon like this before.

‘Good heavens!’ the Duchess said to herself. ‘So he is some sort of foot doctor after all. How dreadful. I hope at least he is a foreigner. That would make it a little less awful.’

‘I really must introduce him to you.’

‘Introduce him!’ exclaimed the Duchess. ‘You cannot mean he is here?’ She began searching for a small tortoiseshell fan and a badly torn lace shawl, so she could leave at a moment’s notice.

‘Of course he is here. I would never think of giving a party without him. He says I have a purely psychic hand, and that if my thumb had been even a tiny bit shorter, I would have become a hopeless pessimist and entered a convent.’

‘Oh, I understand!’ said the Duchess, greatly relieved. ‘He tells fortunes, I suppose?’

‘And misfortunes as well,’ Lady Windermere replied. ‘As many as you like. Next year, for example, I face terrible dangers both on land and at sea, so I mean to live in a balloon and pull my dinner up in a basket each evening. It is all written on my little finger, or perhaps the palm of my hand. I forget which.’

‘But surely that is tempting Providence, Gladys.’

‘My dear Duchess, surely Providence has learned to resist temptation by now. I think everyone ought to have their palm read once a month, to know what they should avoid doing. Naturally, we do it anyway, but being warned is so pleasant. Now, unless someone fetches Mr. Podgers immediately, I shall have to go myself.’

‘Let me fetch him, Lady Windermere,’ said a tall, handsome young man nearby, who had been listening with an amused smile.

‘Thank you so much, Lord Arthur, but I fear you would not recognise him.’

‘If he is as wonderful as you say, Lady Windermere, surely I cannot miss him. Describe him to me, and I shall bring him straight over.’

‘Well, he looks nothing like a palm reader. I mean he has no mysterious, secretive, or romantic air. He is a short, plump man with a funny bald head and huge gold-rimmed glasses. He looks somewhere between a family doctor and a country lawyer. I am terribly sorry, but that is hardly my fault. People are so irritating. Every one of my pianists looks exactly like a poet, and every poet looks exactly like a pianist. Last season I remember inviting a dreadful conspirator to dinner—a man who had blown up any number of people, always wore chain mail, and kept a dagger hidden up his shirtsleeve. And do you know, when he arrived he looked just like a kindly old clergyman, and spent the whole evening making jokes?

“The bewilderment and astonishment occasioned in my mind by this extraordinary alteration in our circumstances was perhaps, of all the adventure, the portion most difficult to explain. For the reversal itself was not merely natural and unavoidable, but had long been foreseen as an event to be looked for when I reached that precise stage of my journey at which the planet’s attraction would yield to that of its satellite—or, to speak more accurately, when the balloon’s gravitation toward the earth would become weaker than its gravitation toward the moon. Certainly I had awakened from a deep sleep, my senses wholly confused, to behold a most startling phenomenon, which, though anticipated, had not been anticipated at that instant. The turning itself must naturally have occurred gently and by degrees; and it is far from certain that, even had I been awake when it happened, any internal indication of an inversion would have alerted me—that is, any discomfort or disturbance affecting either my own person or my equipment.

“It scarcely requires saying that, once I had properly understood my position and escaped the terror that had occupied every faculty of my soul, my attention first became entirely absorbed in examining the moon’s general physical aspect. It stretched below me like a chart; and although I estimated that a considerable distance still separated us, the hollows of its surface appeared to my eyes with a remarkably striking and wholly inexplicable clarity. At first sight, the most extraordinary feature of its geological state seemed the complete lack of ocean or sea, or indeed any lake, river, or other body of water. Yet, curiously enough, I could distinguish immense level tracts of unmistakably alluvial character, though much the larger share of the visible hemisphere was overlaid with countless volcanic mountains, shaped like cones and resembling artificial elevations rather than natural ones. The loftiest of these rises no more than three and three-quarter miles vertically; but a chart of the volcanic regions of the Campi Phlegraei would convey to your Excellencies a better conception of their general appearance than any inadequate account I might venture to offer. Most of them were plainly erupting, and made me fearfully aware of their violence and strength through the repeated thunder of the stones incorrectly termed meteoric, which now hurtled upward past the balloon with an increasingly dreadful frequency.”
